maxPerMinute.hint: Per person, per conversation. Thirty stops a flood without ever meeting somebody typing. Zero for as many as they can type.

spamGuard.label: Spam protection
spamGuard.hint: Limits loose enough that nobody talking normally meets them, there to stop clear abuse: the whole room pinged again and again, one person mentioned over and over, the same line pasted repeatedly. Each counts one person in one conversation; zero turns a single limit off.

maxRoomMentionsPerHour.label: @everyone and @here
maxRoomMentionsPerHour.hint: Messages carrying either that one person may send in an hour. Whoever moderates the room is not held by it.

maxMentionsPerMessage.label: People mentioned in one message
maxMentionsPerMessage.hint: Different people or teams one message may mention.

maxSamePersonMentions.label: Mentioning the same person
maxSamePersonMentions.hint: Messages mentioning the same person that one account may send in ten minutes.

maxRepeatedMessages.label: The same message again
maxRepeatedMessages.hint: How many times the very same message may be sent in two minutes.

maxAttachments.label: Files on one message
maxAttachments.hint: Zero stops files being sent in this kind of conversation at all.

maxAttachmentMib.label: Biggest single file
maxAttachmentMib.hint: A file this big is streamed straight to the storage Polaris writes uploads to, so what this really sets is how much of your disks one message may take. Somebody sharing a file they already have in Drive is not bound by it at all when this instance shares by link.

editWindowMinutes.label: How long a message stays editable
editWindowMinutes.hint: Minutes after it was sent. Zero means always, which is what people expect. It covers deleting too, and never binds somebody moderating the room.

deleteLeavesTrace.label: Deleting leaves a line saying so
deleteLeavesTrace.hint: On, a deleted message reads 'This message was deleted' and replies under it still make sense. Off, the message and its files go without trace - except for one that has replies hanging off it, which would take them with it.

keepEditHistory.label: Keep what a message said before it was edited
keepEditHistory.hint: On, '(edited)' opens the earlier versions for anybody who can read the message. Off, no earlier version is recorded from then on.

copy.label: Copied

link.hint: Shared where it already is. Nothing is copied, so any size works and the limit above does not apply - but whoever owns the file can edit it or delete it under a message that has already been read, and the conversation says so on the file.

orgChat.label: Organizations may keep their own chat
orgChat.hint: An organization that takes this gets a second chat for the people in it, reached from the shelf switch in the header. Turned off, everybody shares one chat - and any organization already keeping its own has those conversations folded back into it rather than hidden.

call.stoppedNote: The call server is not answering, so these ports carry nothing yet and cannot be checked. Chat settings says what it is doing.
call.onlyLocal: Calls only reach this network so far
call.nothingArrived: Nothing has arrived on the call ports from outside yet. Forwarding them in the router fixes it, and this ticks itself the moment they work.

call.address: The address callers are sent to

call.addressBody: The call server asks for it once, when it starts, and hands it out until it restarts. If this line's address changes, calls from outside go quiet while everything here stays green.

Their events then appear in the Tasks calendar, read-only, and they can sign in with the account they linked if you allow it. Polaris never holds a credential that reaches everybody's calendar - only the access each person granted.

0.label: Fill in the consent screen
0.help: Google refuses to create a client until this exists. Audience: External, unless everybody here is in the same Workspace. Name the app exactly Polaris - verification compares it against the name on the home page - and give it these three URLs and the logo.

1.label: Add the authorized domain
1.help: Same page, under Authorized domains. Every URL above has to sit on it, and Google rejects an IP address outright - this needs a domain name.

2.label: Prove you own the domain
2.help: Verification refuses a home page that is 'not registered to you'. Add the domain in Search Console, signed in as the account that owns this Cloud project, and complete the DNS check it gives you.

3.label: Create an OAuth client
3.help: Application type: Web application. Google has no way to pre-fill the form, so paste this into Authorized redirect URIs.

4.label: Enable the Calendar API
4.help: On the same project. Without it the client authorizes fine and every calendar comes back empty.

5.label: Enable the Tasks API
5.help: Same project. It puts each person's Google Tasks on their calendar; without it the calendars still sync, with no tasks.

6.label: Publish the app
6.help: A new client is in Testing, where only the accounts listed as test users may authorize and everybody else is refused with access_denied. Publishing lifts that. Until you are ready to, add each person as a test user instead.

7.label: Submit it for verification
7.help: The last step, and the only one that removes the 'Google hasn't verified this app' warning. Reading a calendar is a sensitive scope, so Google wants the pages above, the domain proved, a reason for the scope, and a video of somebody connecting an account. Published but unverified works - everyone just has to click through the warning first.

Polaris holds no credential that reaches anybody's files - only the access each person granted.

steam.description: Steam needs nothing registered: it signs people in over OpenID, so the Connect button on everybody's account works the moment this is switched on. A Web API key is optional and buys one thing - the name and avatar beside a linked account, instead of a seventeen-digit number. An ARK server closed by Steam id can then be opened to somebody by their Polaris name.
steam.apiKeyHelp: Optional. Without it a linked account shows its Steam id rather than its name.

0.label: Get a Web API key

epic.summary: Let people link their Epic account, so game servers can recognize them.
epic.description: Register a product in Epic's developer portal and everyone here gets a Connect button for their own Epic account. Polaris reads the account id and the display name, which is what a server needs to tell one player from another. Games bought on the Epic Store carry no Steam id at all, so for those players this is the only id there is. The longest setup on this screen: Epic wants an application, a verified domain and a brand review before it will let anybody outside your own organization authorize.
epic.apiKeyHelp: Shown once when the client is created, next to its id.

0.label: Create a product
0.help: Everything else hangs off a product, so it is the first thing to make. The organization it belongs to is created with your account.

1.label: Create a client, and register the redirect URI on it
1.help: Product settings -> Clients -> New client. Policy type Custom with 'User required' ticked, which is what a client that signs a person in needs; leave every feature disabled, since Polaris only reads who authorized. Paste this into its redirect URLs.

2.label: Create the application and link the client to it
2.help: Product settings -> Epic Account Services. Brand settings take the name, the 128x128 logo and these URLs; Permissions needs only Basic Profile, which is always on; Linked clients has to name the client you just made, or the two never meet.

3.label: Verify your domain
3.help: Organization settings -> the domain, then the TXT record Epic gives you at your DNS host. Despite the name, the value is public once it is in DNS - it proves the domain is yours and nothing else. The site it points at has to be reachable without signing in and name your organization and product; the home page above does.

4.label: Save the draft, then submit it for review
4.help: Until it passes, only accounts in your own organization can authorize - everybody else is turned away, and your own sees an unverified warning it can click through. That is enough to finish this setup and prove it works; the review is what opens it to everyone else.

5.label: Copy the client id and secret
5.help: Product settings -> SDK download and credentials, which lists every client. The secret is shown when the client is created; if it was not kept, make a new client rather than guessing.

Once it is connected, linking an account hands Polaris the username as Mojang spells it - which is exactly what a server's player list is keyed by.

discord.summary: Let people link their Discord account, so game servers can recognize them.
discord.description: Register an application in Discord's developer portal and everyone here gets a Connect button for their own Discord account. Polaris reads the account id and the name they go by, which is what a FiveM server's door is keyed by, and records it against their Polaris account instead of leaving it to be read out over chat. It also reads their address and the servers they are in, which is what the consent screen will say. The shortest setup on this screen: an application, a redirect URI, and the secret. Signing in with a Discord account is a separate switch below, and it starts off.
discord.apiKeyHelp: The OAuth2 tab's client secret, shown once when it is reset.

spotify.summary: Let people show what they are listening to, and listen along with each other.
spotify.description: Create an app in Spotify's developer dashboard and everyone here gets a Connect button for their own Spotify. Beside their name, people who share it then see the song they are playing, and can press Listen along to hear it on their own Spotify. Spotify only lets an app control playback for a Premium account, so Listen along says so to anybody without one; showing the song works for everybody. Spotify also requires a secure (https) address for this Polaris, and keeps an app in development mode unless it is approved: in that mode the app's owner needs Premium and only the accounts added under User Management - five at most - can link.

krisp.summary: Use a licensed noise filter in calls instead of the free one.
krisp.description: Calls already remove background noise with two free models that run in the browser and cost nothing. This is for an operator who has licensed a better one - Krisp being the one people ask for, since it is what Discord runs. Krisp does not publish its browser SDK for anyone to install, so what goes here is your own build of it: the address it is served from and the token it authenticates with. Both reach the browser, because that is where a filter on a microphone runs, and only ever a browser sitting in a call.

tenor.summary: Search GIFs and stickers from the chat composer.

Without it the picker still works - emoji, the pictures each person has kept, and anything sent by pasting its address - and only the search tab is missing. A chosen GIF is fetched once and stored here like any other attachment, so a conversation never asks Tenor for anything and nobody is told who read what.

A chosen GIF is fetched once and stored here like any other attachment, so a conversation never asks Giphy for anything and nobody is told who read what.

cloudflare.summary: Create your DNS records and expose apps with no port-forwarding.
cloudflare.description: Connect an API token and Polaris writes your zones' DNS records and gives each app its own tunnel, so nothing is typed into a DNS panel and no ports are opened. One token can do both, or connect DNS and tunnels separately. A connector token can also be pasted here to run a single server-wide tunnel instead.

ngrok.summary: Expose deployed apps through an ngrok tunnel, no port-forwarding.
ngrok.description: Runs an ngrok agent from this server that forwards inbound traffic to Polaris. Good for quick public access; a reserved domain (ngrok paid) is recommended for a stable URL.

duckdns.summary: Free dynamic DNS - keep a subdomain pointed at your changing IP.
duckdns.description: Points a free '<name>'.duckdns.org subdomain at this server's public IP and keeps it updated as your ISP address changes, so a home box stays reachable. DuckDNS also resolves *.'<name>'.duckdns.org, so it works as a wildcard base for app subdomains.

run.starting: The update is starting; waiting for it to report.
run.reattached: Reattached to an update already running.
run.neverReported: An update was running at {at} and never reported a result. It may still be going, or it may have been cut off.
run.lastFailed: The last update failed (exit code {code}). See the log below.
run.reportFailed: Could not prepare the report. The log above can be attached to an issue by hand.
run.started: The dashboard keeps serving while the new build starts; this page reloads when it takes over.
run.unavailable: This installation cannot update itself from here: it was set up without the part that installs updates. It updates only by installing it again, the same way it was installed. Your data and settings are kept, and this button works from then on.
run.disabled: Updates were switched off for this machine when it was set up, so Polaris does not install them, from here or on a schedule.
run.unreachable: The part of Polaris that installs updates is not answering. It restarts on its own, so try again in a minute. In the limited edition it is not there at all, and Polaris updates only by installing it again.
run.slow: This is taking longer than expected. The log above is still the live one.
run.noLiveLog: Updating - this host writes no live log. Reconnecting when Polaris is back...
run.serving: The new build is serving - reloading...
run.failed: Update failed (exit code {code}). See the log below.
run.failedUnknown: Update failed (exit code unknown). See the log below.

publicPages.title: Public pages
publicPages.intro: Everything else here is behind the login. These three are not, because a service you register an OAuth client with will not verify one it cannot read - Google refuses a home page behind a sign-in, and asks for the privacy policy and terms on the same domain.
publicPages.contactHint: An address or a link, shown on the privacy and terms pages as the way to reach whoever runs this deployment. Left empty, those pages carry no contact at all.
